metadata.title: Expected 665.24, Observed 630
metadata.topic: INFO 7375 WEEK 1 - RANDOMNESS AND FIRST PROMPTS
metadata.author: Prathamesh P
metadata.note: Week 1 explainer. One concept: expected count (1000 x 0.6652409557748218 = 665.24) vs observed count (630) for token 2 in the seed-7 run of lessons/01-randomness-and-first-prompts/code/main.py (course repo b293224, Python 3.11.9, run 2026-09-27). No Claude interface, no instructor persona, no channel chip or logo (student decision; see FRICTIONAL.md). Counters only, no equation beats (course prerequisite guide takes priority). Narration signed at GATE P by the student - see PEDAGOGY.md.

beats.narration_text: Same program, same token, same run. One number says 665.24. The other says 630. Neither is a mistake. They answer different questions.
beats.visual_intent: Two large numbers side by side, each with its provenance label.

show.at: Same program, same token, same run
show.event: kicker line types in: same program, same token, same run
665.24 rises in on the left; label: expected count, computed 1000 x p(token 2), main.py
630 rises in on the right; label: observed count, main.py output, seed 7
a question mark under each: what chance was assigned? / what happened this run?

beats.narration_text: The distribution expects 665.24 draws of token two. One seeded run of a thousand gave 630. Read the first as a promise, and the second looks like a bug. It isn't.
beats.visual_intent: Hesitant writer types the misconception and corrects it; corner banner labels it a constructed example.

props.text:
The code predicts
665 of token 2.
One seeded run of 1,000 draws gave 630.
props.brandLabel: Narration: synthetic voice (Kokoro af_bella), not the author

show.event: writer types 'The code predicts 665 of token 2.' - code, predicts and 665 are each reconsidered and replaced
corrected line stands: 'The distribution expects 665.24 of token 2.'
second line complete: 'One seeded run of 1,000 draws gave 630.'

beats.narration_text: This is the whole mechanism, from the course's main.py. Scores one, two, three become probabilities, and token two gets about sixty-six and a half percent. Then a generator seeded with seven makes a thousand weighted draws.
beats.visual_intent: Real main.py excerpt beside three probability bars built from its actual output.

show.event: real code excerpt of probabilities() and sample() appears, source line labelled
token 2 bar is the one accent
the rng.choices(..., k=count) line and Random(seed) highlight

beats.narration_text: Multiply that probability by a thousand: 665.24. That's an expected count, the average number of token twos you would see across many runs of a thousand draws. It isn't even a whole number, so no single run can land on it. A count is an integer.
beats.visual_intent: Counter rolls from 0 to 665.24; the other expected counts follow; the .24 is flagged as not an integer.

show.event: counter rolls to 665.24
expected counts for all three tokens: 90.03, 244.73, 665.24 (labelled computed from main.py output)
the .24 is boxed: not an integer

beats.narration_text: Now the real draws, in order. The first is token one, not the favorite. Token two first appears on draw three. Nothing reserves a quota; each draw is weighted and independent. After a thousand: 102, 268, 630.
beats.visual_intent: The real seed-7 sequence fills three bins draw by draw, slow at first then fast, ending at 102 / 268 / 630.

show.event: draw 1 drops into the token 1 bin
draw 3 drops into token 2, marked: first token 2
remaining draws stream in from the real sequence, counters climbing
counters land on 102, 268, 630

beats.narration_text: Side by side: token zero came up about twelve more times than expected, token one about twenty-three more, token two about thirty-five fewer. The gaps cancel, because both rows total a thousand. The probability is the chance assigned; the count is what this sample did.
beats.visual_intent: Expected (outline) vs observed (filled) bars per token, with the three gaps and their zero sum.

show.event: token 0 pair with gap +11.97
token 1 pair with gap +23.27
token 2 pair with gap -35.24
gaps sum line: +11.97 + 23.27 - 35.24 = 0.00; both rows total 1000
probability 0.6652 vs observed share 0.630 for token 2

beats.narration_text: Run it again with seed seven on this machine: 630 again, byte for byte. A seed makes the run repeatable. It doesn't pull the count toward 665, and it doesn't make 630 more correct.
beats.visual_intent: The two real saved outputs side by side with matching SHA-256.

show.event: run 1 output file appears, then run 2 beside it
both SHA-256 lines appear and match: identical
the 630 in both panels stays put

beats.narration_text: Here's what this can't tell you. One seed-seven run of a thousand draws cannot show whether a gap of 35.24 is typical. To call it broken, or normal, you need an acceptance criterion. A single run cannot give you that criterion. You have to decide it first.
beats.visual_intent: One real point at -35.24 on a constructed axis whose other slots are marked not measured.

show.event: heading: What this does not establish
one dot at -35.24 on the gap axis (seed 7); other slots dashed: not measured
an empty criterion box appears on the axis
box label: decide before you look

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Before you run anything, write down how far from 665 is too far. Then run the course's sample function with twenty other seeds and list token two's count. Check them against your rule, and notice if you're tempted to move it.
beats.visual_intent: Plain card: the suggested experiment, the tested snippet, and the folder to run it from.

show.event: heading: Your turn
the rule prompt appears with an empty line to fill
3-line snippet and run-from folder appear; label: suggestion, results not shown
the empty rule line pulses once

beats.narration_text: Expected, 665.24. Observed, 630. Two numbers, two questions. Keep both.
beats.visual_intent: Title restate, author, provenance and narration disclosure.
